title: Fight for the faith, keep yourselves, show mercy
sum: Jude meant to write a warm letter about "the salvation we share." Instead he sends an urgent warning: people have slipped into the church who turn God's grace into an excuse for indulgence and deny Jesus as Master. Jude does not argue with their ideas. He reminds his readers of a long line of rebels and their fate: Israel in the wilderness, the angels who left heaven, Sodom, Cain, Balaam and Korah. Then he quotes a prophecy of Enoch and the apostles' warnings: "These are the people."

The last third of the letter turns to the faithful. Build yourselves up, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love, and wait for Christ's mercy. Then show mercy to others: steady those who waver, snatch some out of the fire, and pity others carefully. The letter ends with one of the best-loved blessings in the Bible: praise to the God who is able to guard you from tripping.

Jude is short but dense. Almost every line alludes to the Old Testament or to Jewish tradition, including two books outside the Bible, 1 Enoch and the Assumption of Moses. Below the views are deep dives on Jude's method, his use of those books, the overlap with 2 Peter, and the two hardest manuscript problems in the letter.
readings: Read historically, Jude is an emergency note to a real congregation, probably of Jewish Christians who knew 1 Enoch and the stories of the wilderness. Wandering teachers have arrived, claim visions, eat at the church's meals and live without restraint. Jude's job is to name the danger and to steady the church, quickly.
Read as a sermon on Scripture

Read literarily, verses 5–19 are a carefully built commentary. Jude sets out a "text" (a type from Scripture or a prophecy) and then applies it: "these are..." (1:8, 10, 12, 16, 19). It is the style of the Dead Sea Scrolls' commentaries, which quote a prophecy and then say "its interpretation concerns..." The structure is the message: what was written long ago (1:4) is happening now.

Many readers find Jude harsh. Its core, though, is pastoral: the faith is a gift to protect, not a weapon, and the letter ends by telling readers to rescue and pity those being pulled away, while relying on God, not themselves, to keep them standing.

views.T: A brother of Jesus writes, perhaps in the 50s or 60s, to Jewish-Christian churches troubled by libertine teachers. The examples and the Enoch quotation are true warnings from God's past dealings. Jude 5's "Jesus" (if original) shows a high view of Christ very early.
views.C: Probably written late in the first century, possibly in Jude's name by a later Christian. The opponents may be early Gnostics or radical Paulinists, and "the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (1:3) reflects a church settling its doctrine. Some scholars call this "early catholicism"; others answer that nothing in Jude requires a late date.
views.J: A Jewish-Christian midrash: Jude reads Scripture and 1 Enoch the way Palestinian Jews of his time did, links texts by catchwords ("ungodly," "keep," "these"), and treats the present as the last time foretold by the prophets. Richard Bauckham's work made this reading influential, and it supports an early date in Palestinian Christianity.

deep.b:
Verses 5–19 alternate between texts and applications. Each "text" is a type from Scripture or a prophecy, mostly in the past tense. Each application begins with "these" (houtoi) and uses the present tense:

  • Text: three judgments, Israel, the angels, Sodom (1:5–7). Application: "these dreamers..." (1:8).
  • Text: Michael and the devil (1:9). Application: "these people slander..." (1:10).
  • Text: Cain, Balaam, Korah (1:11). Application: "these people are sunken rocks..." (1:12–13).
  • Text: Enoch's prophecy (1:14–15). Application: "These people are grumblers..." (1:16).
  • Text: the apostles' prophecy (1:17–18). Application: "These people draw dividing lines" (1:19).

This is close to the pesher style of the Dead Sea Scrolls, where a commentary quotes a prophecy and then explains how it is being fulfilled in the writer's own community. Words link the texts together: "ungodly" (1:4, 15, 18), "judgment" (1:4, 6, 9, 15), "keep" (1:1, 6, 13, 21), "slander" (1:8, 9, 10). Jude also loves threes: called, loved and kept (1:1); mercy, peace and love (1:2); three judgments (1:5–7); three charges (1:8); three rebels (1:11); three groups to help (1:22–23).

deep.h: Jude's library: 1 Enoch and the Assumption of Moses
deep.b:
Jude quotes or retells three things that are not in the Old Testament:

  • The Watchers (1:6): angels who left heaven for human women, from 1 Enoch's retelling of Genesis 6:1–4.
  • Michael and the devil (1:9): a dispute over Moses's body, which early writers said came from the Assumption of Moses.
  • Enoch's prophecy (1:14–15): a direct quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9.

1 Enoch was widely read by Jews of Jude's time: the Dead Sea Scrolls include fragments of several copies, in Aramaic. Early Christians such as the writer of the Epistle of Barnabas, Irenaeus and Tertullian knew it well. Jude calls Enoch's words prophecy, which made later Christians uneasy. Some thought Jude must be wrong to quote such a book; Tertullian thought Jude's quotation proved the book was good. Most churches settled on a middle view: Jude cited a true prophecy without making the whole book Scripture. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, whose Bible contains 1 Enoch, took the other road.

Almost all of Jude 4–18 reappears in 2 Peter 2:1–3:3, in nearly the same order: the intruders who deny the Master, the angels, Sodom, slander of glorious ones, the angels' restraint, animals without reason, Balaam, the feasts, waterless clouds, darkness reserved, swollen words, and the apostles' warning about mockers. Most scholars conclude that 2 Peter used Jude: Jude's version is tighter, and 2 Peter leaves out the material from 1 Enoch and the Assumption of Moses, which a later writer might avoid. A minority thinks Jude used 2 Peter, and some suggest both used shared preaching. See the topic page for the full list of parallels.

The manuscripts of 1:5 say four different things: "Jesus," "the Lord," "God," or (in Papyrus 72) "God Christ." For decades most editions printed "the Lord," though Bruce Metzger argued for "Jesus" in a famous dissent. Since 2012 the main critical editions (NA28 and the Editio Critica Maior) read "Jesus." English Bibles are divided: the ESV, CSB, NLT, NET, NRSVue and BSB read "Jesus"; the KJV, NKJV, NIV, NASB and NABRE read "the Lord." Ancient scribes abbreviated these names in two letters, ΙΣ and ΚΣ, which made confusion easy. If Jude wrote "Jesus," he believed that the one who rescued Israel was the Son of God, active in Israel's history before his human birth, as Paul says of the rock in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:4). Switch the reading in the text to see each version.

These two verses survive in at least five forms. The main ones are: three groups (have mercy on some who waver; save others by snatching them from the fire; on others have mercy with fear), in Codex Sinaiticus and the main modern editions; three groups with "correct" instead of the first "have mercy," in Codex Alexandrinus; two groups in the Byzantine text and KJV ("of some have compassion, making a difference; and others save with fear"); and a short two-group form in Papyrus 72 ("snatch some from the fire, but on those who waver [or: dispute] have mercy with fear"), which Richard Bauckham argues is original, reading "those who dispute." The three-group form fits Jude's love of threes, but the repeated "have mercy" is awkward. Whichever is original, Jude's point is clear: the readers must actively rescue people, not only defend themselves.

Jude describes their behavior, not their doctrine. They claimed revelations (1:8), lived without moral restraint and called it grace (1:4), mocked angelic powers (1:8–10), sought money and influence (1:11, 16), ate at the church's meals (1:12), and treated themselves as the spiritual elite (1:19). Proposals include: early Gnostics, who in the 100s divided people into "spiritual" and "natural" classes; radical followers of Paul who took "freedom from the law" to an extreme (compare 1 Corinthians 6:12); or wandering charismatic prophets like those the Didache warns about. Most recent commentators think a full Gnostic system is too late and too specific; the description fits a looser antinomian ("against the law") movement.

deep.title: "Lord" means Jesus all through Jude
deep.body: My theory: Jude consistently reads Old Testament "Lord" (God) texts as speaking of Jesus. He calls Jesus "our only Master and Lord" (1:4), uses the name "Jesus" for the God of the Exodus (1:5, if original), and inserts "the Lord" into Enoch's prophecy of God's coming (1:14). Even Michael's "The Lord rebuke you" (1:9), from Zechariah 3:2 where the speaker is the LORD himself, may be heard as an appeal to Jesus. If this pattern is deliberate, it is an argument from inside the letter for "Jesus" in 1:5: the harder reading fits Jude's own habit. Jarl Fossum (1987) argued that Jude identifies Jesus with the angel of the LORD in 1:5–7, and Bauckham notes Jude's insertion of "Lord" in 1:14; my addition is to read the four together as one deliberate pattern.

echoes: Genesis 4:3–16; Genesis 5:18–24; Genesis 6:1–4; Isaiah 24:21–22; Genesis 19:1–29; Numbers 14:20–35; Numbers 16:1–35; Numbers 22–24; Numbers 31:16; Deuteronomy 33:2; Deuteronomy 34:5–6; Proverbs 25:14; Isaiah 57:20; Ezekiel 34:2; Zechariah 3:1–5; Zechariah 14:5; Daniel 10:13; Romans 6:1–2; Romans 16:25–27; 1 Corinthians 10:1–12; 1 Corinthians 2:14; 2 Peter 2:1–22; 2 Peter 3:2–3; Revelation 2:14; Revelation 12:7

settings.to: the churches he writes to, called "the people who have been called, who are loved in God the Father and kept safe for Jesus Christ"
settings.when: at the opening of the letter, before the warning
settings.why: Jude names himself by his brother James, the leader of the Jerusalem church, which gives his word weight with Jewish-Christian readers. The three words for the readers (called, loved, kept) set the theme of the whole letter. The intruders are "kept" for judgment (1:6, 1:13), but the faithful are kept by God, and at the end he will "guard you from tripping" (1:24). The wish for "mercy" and "love" returns in the charge of 1:21–23.

settings.to: the believers of these churches, whom he calls "beloved," about teachers who had come in among them
settings.when: after news that the intruders were already at the churches' love feasts, so that Jude set aside the letter he had planned
settings.why: Jude does not debate the intruders. He sets each example from the past next to "these people" in the present: Israel saved from Egypt and later judged, the angels who left their place, Sodom, then Cain, Balaam and Korah. The point for the readers is that welcome and status in the church do not protect anyone who turns grace into license. The story of Michael and the devil (1:9), which early writers (Clement of Alexandria, Origen) say came from the Assumption of Moses, a book now partly lost, shames the intruders' slander of angels: even the archangel left judgment to the Lord. The images of 1:12–13 (sunken rocks, or "stains" as some read the word, clouds with no rain, dead trees, foaming waves, wandering stars) warn that these teachers promise much and give nothing, and they are dangerous at the very meals where the church shows its love.
views: Most readers see the intruders as teachers who used freedom in Christ as a license for sexual sin and rejected moral authority.

Some older critical scholars saw them as early Gnostics who claimed spiritual visions and despised the body and the angels who gave the law. Many now think Jude's words fit a looser and earlier movement.

settings.to: the same churches, who knew and valued the Book of Enoch
settings.when: as the climax of the warning, after the woe on Cain, Balaam and Korah
settings.why: Jude quotes a prophecy his readers already honored. In 1 Enoch the words describe God coming to judge the wicked. Jude adds the word "Lord" and probably reads it as Jesus (some think he means God), and "the ungodly" as the intruders, whose "harsh words" and grumbling show they are the ones Enoch saw. Most scholars think Jude took the words as true prophecy. For readers who honored the book, this was strong proof: an ancient prophet from before the flood had already named their kind and their end. The repeated word "ungodly" (four times in 1:15) ties the prophecy to Jude's charge in 1:4.
views: Many scholars think Jude believed Enoch's words were truly from God, even if he did not count the whole book as Scripture.
Others stress that Jude quotes it because his readers, and maybe the intruders, prized it, as Paul quotes Greek poets in Acts 17:28.

settings.to: the believers who had not been led astray, "you, beloved"
settings.when: after the warning, as the letter turns from the intruders to the readers
settings.why: This is the heart of the letter and what Jude most wanted them to do. First he reminds them that the apostles had warned of "mockers" in the last time, so the crisis should not shake their faith. Then he gives four commands: build yourselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love, and look for Christ's mercy. Last, he tells them how to treat others in the church: have mercy on those who waver, pull some out of the fire, and show mercy with fear to others, without being stained by their sin. The letter that began as an alarm ends as a call to rescue, not to drive people out.
views: Ancient manuscripts differ in 1:22–23. Some have three groups (waverers, those in the fire, the stained), others two. Either way, Jude asks for mercy toward people caught by the intruders.

settings.to: the churches, likely read aloud when they gathered for worship
settings.when: at the close of the letter, in place of greetings
settings.why: Jude ends with praise, not a final warning. After so much about falling and judgment, the readers hear that God "is able to guard you from tripping" and will bring them before his glory "shouting for joy." The words answer the fear the letter might raise: their safety rests on God, who keeps them, as the greeting promised. The form, praise ending in "Amen," comes from Jewish prayer, so the church would know to join in it.

traditions.q: Jude quotes 1 Enoch as prophecy (1:14–15). Is 1 Enoch Scripture?
views: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches say yes: 1 Enoch (with Jubilees) is in their Bible and is read as the word of God, and Jude's quotation is one reason. The other Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Armenian, Syriac) do not include it, so this family of churches is itself divided.

No. Augustine said Enoch surely wrote some things inspired by God, since Jude says so, but the books under his name were rightly left out because no one could be sure they were his. The canon fixed at Trent (1546) does not include 1 Enoch.

No. The Greek Bible of the Eastern Orthodox churches never included 1 Enoch, though the fathers knew its stories. Jude shows that a true prophecy could be kept outside the Old Testament, not that the whole book is holy.

No, and Luther doubted Jude itself for quoting it. In his preface of 1522 he said Jude cites sayings and stories found nowhere in Scripture, which is why the early church held the letter back from the chief books.

No. The Westminster Confession says books outside the canon have no authority in the church beyond other human writings. Jude quoted a true saying from a non-biblical book the way Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12), and the Spirit's use of one line does not make the rest Scripture.

traditions.q: What is "the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (1:3), and where is it kept?
views: It is the deposit of faith, which Christ gave to the apostles and which reaches us in two ways: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition. The bishops in union with the pope (the Magisterium) guard and explain it, and no new public revelation will be added before Christ returns (Catechism 66, 84).

It is Holy Tradition, the one life of the Holy Spirit in the church. Scripture is the heart of that Tradition, together with the creeds, the councils, the liturgy and the fathers, and the whole church, not one bishop, keeps it.

The faith once handed down is now found in the written word. The Formula of Concord calls Scripture "the only rule and norm" for judging all teachers; the creeds and confessions are trusted witnesses to that faith, not a second source.

The Westminster Confession says the whole counsel of God is set down in Scripture, and nothing is to be added to it, whether by new revelations of the Spirit or by human traditions. "Once for all" means the faith is complete.

The faith is complete in Scripture, which is the final rule. But Pentecostals expect the Spirit to keep speaking through prophecy, tongues and other gifts today, always tested by Scripture and never adding to it, so they do not read "once for all" as an end to the gifts.

traditions.q: Jude says "keep yourselves in God's love" (1:21) and praises the God who is able to guard you from tripping (1:24). Can a true believer fall away for good?
views: No. The Canons of Dort and the Westminster Confession teach that those God has truly called can neither totally nor finally fall from grace. The command in verse 21 is real, but it is the means by which God's promise in verse 24 is kept.

Most Baptist confessions say no: "All true believers endure to the end" (Baptist Faith and Message, article 5; the 1689 London Confession says the same). Free Will Baptists and some others disagree and hold that a believer can fall away.

Yes. Wesley argued that a real believer can make shipwreck of faith, and that Jude would not command people to keep themselves in God's love if there were no danger of leaving it. God guards those who keep trusting him.

Yes. The Augsburg Confession (article 12) rejects the teaching that people once justified cannot lose the Holy Spirit. Yet Lutherans stress that God's promise is sure, and that falling away comes from turning from it, not from any weakness in it.
Yes. Grace can be lost by mortal sin and restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance, and staying faithful to the end is itself a gift to pray for (Catechism 1861).

traditions.q: Sodom suffers "the punishment of eternal fire" (1:7). Is final punishment endless conscious suffering?
views: Yes. The Church teaches that hell exists and is eternal, and that its chief pain is eternal separation from God, for whom we were made (Catechism 1035). The "eternal fire" is real, though what it is like is not described.
Yes. The Westminster Confession says the wicked will be cast into eternal torments and punished with everlasting destruction. Most Baptist and many evangelical confessions say the same.

Yes, but Orthodox writers often describe the fire as God's own love and glory, which is joy to those who love him and torment to those who refuse him (Isaac the Syrian). Some Orthodox theologians dare to hope that all may at last be saved, though the church condemned the teaching that all surely will be (553).

Divided. Many Anglicans hold the traditional view, while John Stott leaned toward the view that the lost are finally destroyed, and a Church of England report (1995) described hell as total non-being rather than endless torment.

No. Adventists teach that the soul is not naturally immortal and that the wicked will be destroyed by fire at the end. Sodom's fire was "eternal" in its result: it destroyed the cities for good, but it is not still burning.
